paper_metadata.title: A Systematic Literature Review on RDF Triple Generation from Natural Language Texts
paper_metadata.abstract: Systematic literature review of methods that generate RDF triples and enhance knowledge graphs from natural-language texts. It retrieved and categorized 150 articles, analyzes challenges and limitations, reports a recent transformer trend, and identifies research gaps and future directions.

problem_addressed: The paper reviews how unstructured natural-language text can be transformed into RDF subject-predicate-object triples and integrated into an existing ontology-governed knowledge graph; it characterizes methods, benefits, drawbacks, inputs/outputs, automation, applications, and T-Box/A-Box population.

methodology.primary_family: Not applicable — systematic literature review, not a Text-to-KG extraction system
secondary_families: Ontology-constrained and schema-guided methods (survey categories: T-Box and A-Box population)
Validation, correction, and knowledge-fusion methods (reviewed challenge area)
methodology.description: The authors define six research questions; construct Boolean searches over generation/extraction/construction/population × triples/KG/KB × natural-language/unstructured/textual data; search ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, Elsevier Scopus, and ACL Anthology; screen title and abstracts; apply inclusion/exclusion rules; have 15 graduate students review ten articles each with author double-checking; categorize papers, generate metadata, filter the 150 retrieved records to 15 closely aligned papers, then report quantitative, qualitative, and category-based synthesis. The review categories are language specificity, transformer use, T-Box/A-Box population, lexical resources, domain specificity, and link creation.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The survey formalizes ontology O as classes, properties, and relationships (T-Box), treats an RDF KG as triples governed by that ontology, and analyzes both T-Box population (new classes/properties) and A-Box population (new instances). It does not itself execute ontology alignment or KG insertion.

input_output.input_type: Input to this study: scientific articles returned by database searches. Target phenomenon reviewed: unstructured natural-language texts, including web pages, social-media posts, and unstructured textual documents.
input_output.input_granularity: For the reviewed systems, text can range from sentences to documents; the paper's formal problem defines a set of textual documents T = {t1, t2, ..., tn}. For the review itself, the unit is an article, initially screened by title and abstract then read in depth.
input_output.output_representation: The surveyed task output is RDF triples in <subject, predicate, object> form, inserted into an existing KG to produce enhanced KG′ = KG ∪ ST. The paper itself outputs a systematic categorization and quantitative/qualitative literature synthesis.

models_and_tools: Literature-search sources: ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, Elsevier Scopus, ACL Anthology
Review workflow: manual/collaborative reading, author double-checking, categorical metadata analysis
Surveyed technical categories include rule-based OpenIE/SRL and transformer-based methods; these are reviewed, not run by this paper
datasets: Review corpus: 150 articles retrieved from six scientific databases
Detailed focused subset: 15 articles that process NL text, generate RDF triples, and integrate them into an existing ontology-constrained KG

metrics: Review-level descriptive counts by publication year, category, domain, source database, automation level, real-world use, data availability, and evaluation type
No Text-to-KG model performance metric is computed by this survey
evaluation.setting: Systematic literature review executed with searches current to August 2023. Inclusion allowed English book chapters, conference papers, journals, and theses that create, use, or theoretically define text-to-triple generation; exclusions covered papers more than ten years old, duplicates, short papers, absent abstracts, non-English works, and works merely mentioning a tool. Fifteen graduate students reviewed ten papers each, and authors double-checked assessments. The study reports descriptive/bibliometric and qualitative synthesis rather than a held-out model benchmark.

value: The authors retrieved 150 articles, organized them in 10 categories, and selected 15 closely focused articles for detailed discussion.
The review reports a rising publication trend from 2019–2022 and identifies transformers as one of the most used techniques in the literature.
A-Box population and English-specific studies are more common, whereas multilingual and link-creation categories have fewer studies.
The surveyed work uses varied evaluation types; quantitative evaluation, especially using gold standards, is reported as common, but no common gold standard was found across the 15 detailed studies.
Most surveyed solutions are automatic or semi-automatic; most do not describe real-world usage or publicly disclose data.

value: Review-level inference: The explicit three-phase protocol, Boolean search formulation, stated eligibility criteria, database list, and reported screening/refinement path make the review more auditable than an unstated narrative survey.

Review-level inference: The paper combines broad quantitative coverage of 150 retrieved articles with detailed, category-based qualitative discussion of 15 papers tightly aligned to ontology-respecting KG enhancement.
Review-level inference: Its categories capture methodological, language, ontology-population, resource, domain, and linking dimensions, enabling comparison beyond a single model family.

value: Review-level inference: The review's evidence base is constrained by English-only eligibility, a ten-year cutoff, six selected databases, and title/abstract screening before full reading; relevant work outside those choices may be missed.

Review-level inference: The detailed synthesis is limited to 15 papers after an initial 150-record analysis, so category-level claims should not be read as a comprehensive benchmark of every retrieved paper.

Review-level inference: It reports a collaborative review and author double-checking but does not report inter-reviewer agreement, a formal quality appraisal score, or a reproducible record-level screening flow in the examined text.
